sections.heading: Why an insider can be a better first PM
sections.content: Rajaram says the first PM often acts as a liaison between founders and the engineering team, so it helps to choose someone both sides trust—someone who already understands how they work. sections.content: Rajaram says first PMs at the companies he had worked at had moved into the role from being an analyst, engineer, or designer. He adds that choosing the right person and giving them good mentors can help them become a good PM in six months.

answer.summary: Rajaram recommends promoting an existing employee because the first PM must bridge founders and engineers, and someone already trusted by both—and familiar with how they work—is more likely to fit culturally and help each side adjust to the role. He accepts that this person may be less strong in PM skills initially; the cultural fit can make the transition work. [S1]

sections.heading: Why promote internally
sections.content: The first PM often acts as the liaison between founders and the engineering team, so Rajaram favors someone both sides trust who already understands how they work. An outside PM may bring a different process that the organization rejects—he describes this as the “organ” being rejected by the “body.” An internal candidate may not have the strongest functional PM skills, but may be a better cultural fit: they can help engineers see the value of a PM and help founders become comfortable gradually handing off work. [S1]
